title: Medhāṃ ma indraḥ: understanding asked of the gods
theme: Medhā is asked of Indra, Sarasvatī and the Aśvins; then the medhā found among the Apsarases, the Gandharvas and the gods is asked to favour the speaker, with svāhā.

words.context: The anonymous commentator: «पुष्करस्रजौ पद्ममालायुक्तावुभावश्विनौ देवौ» — the two Aśvins wearing lotus garlands
The anonymous commentator: «अप्सरासु देवस्त्रीषु» — among the divine women
The anonymous commentator: «गन्धर्वेषु देवगायकेषु» — the singers of the gods
The anonymous commentator: «यन्मनो मेधात्मकमस्ति» — the mind that has the nature of medhā

words.gram: f. acc. sg. as printed (for nom. daivī)
words.context: The anonymous commentator: «दैवीं व्यत्ययेन दैवी» — read as daivī by exchange of case
The anonymous commentator: «सरस्वती वेदशास्त्ररूपा» — in the form of the Vedas and śāstras
The anonymous commentator: «सुरभिः शोभनगन्धा सर्वकामदुघा वा» — sweet-smelling, or yielding every wish

sandhi.type: e before a vowel; aḥ before a voiced sound
sandhi.rule: me + indraḥ → ma indraḥ (P. 6.1.78 (एचोऽयवायावः), P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य)); indraḥ + dadātu → indro dadātu.
au becomes āv before a vowel (P. 6.1.78 (एचोऽयवायावः)).
The m becomes anusvāra before s (P. 8.3.23 (मोऽनुस्वारः)); the Taittirīya recitation writes it ग्.

sandhi_exceptions.note: me · aśvinau: the e of me kept before a without elision (classical me ’śvinau); a Vedic hiatus (prakṛtibhāva, P. 6.1.115 (प्रकृत्यान्तःपादमव्यपरे)), printed so in every witness.

morphology.note: A Vedic dual in -ā for -au, agreeing with aśvinau; the anonymous commentator restores «पुष्करस्रजौ».
Accusative in form where a nominative is meant; the commentator: «दैवीं व्यत्ययेन दैवी».
For apsaraḥsu / apsarassu, from the stem apsaras, treated as an ā-stem.

translation.literal: Medhā may Indra give me; medhā the goddess Sarasvatī; medhā may the two Aśvins, both, place in me, wearing lotus garlands. The medhā that is in the Apsarases, and the mind that is in the Gandharvas, divine medhā, Sarasvatī — may that medhā, the fragrant, favour me. Svāhā.
translation.readable: May Indra give me understanding; may the goddess Sarasvatī give it; may both Aśvins, garlanded with lotuses, set it in me. The understanding of the heavenly nymphs, the mind of the heavenly singers, the understanding of the gods, Sarasvatī herself — may that understanding come to me, fragrant and generous. Svāhā.

anvaya: इन्द्रः मे मेधाम् ददातु । देवी सरस्वती मेधाम् [ददातु] । पुष्करस्रजा उभौ अश्विनौ मे मेधाम् आधत्ताम् । अप्सरासु च या मेधा, गन्धर्वेषु च यत् मनः, दैवीम् मेधा, सरस्वती, सा मेधा सुरभिः माम् जुषताम् । स्वाहा ।
syntax: Two verses. The first: three imperatives (dadātu, said once and understood for Sarasvatī; ādhattām) with medhām as object. The second: relative clauses (yā medhā, yan manaḥ) and appositions resumed by sā … medhā, with the imperative juṣatām and the call svāhā.

ambiguities.note: The anonymous commentator treats the second verse as a further mantra granting medhā («मेधाप्रदं मन्त्रान्तरमाह»); Sāyaṇa comments on the two verses as his anuvākas 40 and 41.
‘Fragrant’ or ‘the wish-yielding cow’; the anonymous commentator gives both.

metre.name: anuṣṭubh
metre.note: Two anuṣṭubh verses, with svāhā at the end outside the metre.

beginner: This short prayer asks several gods for medhā — understanding, and the power to keep what one learns. First Indra, king of the gods; then Sarasvatī, goddess of speech and learning; then the two Aśvins, the twin gods, garlanded with lotuses. The second verse widens the request: the understanding found among the heavenly nymphs, the mind of the heavenly singers, the understanding of the gods, and Sarasvatī herself — may all of it come to me, sweet and generous. It ends with svāhā, the word said when an offering is made into the fire, so the prayer is meant to accompany an offering.
analogy: Like a student writing to several teachers at once, asking each for whatever they can share.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It asks Indra, Sarasvatī and the two Aśvins to give the speaker medhā, and asks the medhā of the Apsarases, the Gandharvas and the gods, Sarasvatī, to favour him, with svāhā.

commentary.q: How do the commentators read it?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator: a prayer to Indra and the others, who grant medhā («मेधाप्रदानिन्द्रादीन्प्रार्थयितुं मन्त्रान्तरमाह»), and then a further mantra that grants medhā, asking the medhā found in the divine women, the mind of the gods’ singers, the medhā of Hiraṇyagarbha and the other gods, and Sarasvatī in the form of the Vedas, to come fragrant and wish-yielding to the speaker. Sāyaṇa reads the same; he adds the medhā of men learned in the Vedas and śāstras («मनुष्यजा मनुष्येषु वेदशास्त्रवित्सु या मेधाऽस्ति»).

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this text is in the edition’s sources; the anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa read it as a prayer for medhā, without a doctrinal argument. Bhāskara’s comment on this part (his anuvākas 39–42) is missing from the edition’s copy, and Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is not among the sources.

contemporary.text: The prayer asks for understanding from many quarters at once — from the gods of power and of speech, and from the twin Aśvins, and from the singers and dancers of heaven. Understanding, it suggests, can be gathered from very different kinds of minds. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: Who are the different people you have learned from, and what did each give you?
reflect.deeper: The verse places medhā among singers and dancers as well as among gods of speech. What kinds of understanding live in music and movement?
reflect.practice: Ask one person today to explain something they know well, and listen.

references.text: Sāyaṇa comments on the two verses as his anuvākas 40 and 41; the edition’s concordance maps both correctly. The base’s ग्स्वाहा (jusatāg svāhā) is the recitation’s spelling of the anusvāra; the other two witnesses write ं, which the collation lists for review.

flags.note: juṣatāg svāhā: the base writes the anusvāra as ग्; the two other witnesses write ं (corrections.json, review). A spelling difference of the recitation; the words are the same.
